claims.source: Natural arm movements recorded to pick and place bottles at those 300 targets were then used to train the ANN involved in our movement-based control (Figure 1c, cf next section), but also to establish a new set of 200 'possible' targets within the workspace actually covered by the participants' arm during the initial acquisition (Figure 1d).
claims.evidence: This describes the generation of test targets.

claims.claim: Anatomical joints' limits are interdependent in a way that makes it uncomfortable or impossible to produce arm configurations with maximal excursion simultaneously at multiple joints.
claims.source: Although 'plausible' targets are all supposed to be reachable, in practice, anatomical joints' limits are interdependent in a way that makes it uncomfortable or impossible to produce arm configurations with maximal excursion simultaneously at multiple joints.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a rationale for the methodology.

claims.claim: An unsupervised self-organizing neural network was used to identify 200 nodes that best represent the arm postures actually produced by participants.
claims.source: To circumvent this, we used an unsupervised self-organizing neural network (Fritzke, 1994) to identify 200 nodes that best represent the arm postures actually produced by participants, and used forward kinematics to turn these nodes into target locations, thereby obtaining a set of 200 possible targets guaranteed to be reachable with natural arm movements (Figure 1d, see Methods).
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology for generating possible targets.

claims.claim: Typical movement times were approximately 1.3 s between pick and place.
claims.source: Video 1 illustrates a participant completing the task at a comfortable yet sustained pace, representative of the overall performance observed in our experiments (i.e. with typical movement times of approximately 1.3 s between pick and place).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a typical performance measure observed in the experiments.

claims.claim: The ANN was trained to reconstruct five distal arm angles from shoulder kinematics plus contextual target information.
claims.source: After being trained to reconstruct five distal arm angles from proximal shoulder kinematics plus target location (3D position and 2D orientation, see Methods), the ANN illustrated in Figure 1c was used to control a Hybrid Arm emulating the behavior of a residual upper arm fitted with a transhumeral prosthesis (Figure 1e).
claims.evidence: This describes the ANN training approach.

claims.claim: Shoulder flexion-extension and abduction-adduction of the Hybrid Arm were operated from real shoulder movements produced by the operator.
claims.source: To this end, shoulder flexion-extension and abduction-adduction of the Hybrid Arm were operated from real shoulder movements produced by the operator, whereas the five remaining joint angles were driven by predictions from the ANN.
claims.evidence: This describes the control scheme for the Hybrid Arm.

claims.claim: The five remaining joint angles of the Hybrid Arm were driven by predictions from the ANN.
claims.source: To this end, shoulder flexion-extension and abduction-adduction of the Hybrid Arm were operated from real shoulder movements produced by the operator, whereas the five remaining joint angles were driven by predictions from the ANN.
claims.evidence: This describes the control scheme for the Hybrid Arm.

claims.claim: The ANN could be trained either solely from the operator's own natural movements (Own ANN) or from those of multiple other participants (Generic ANN).
claims.source: Importantly, the ANN could be trained either solely from the operator's own natural movements (Own ANN, see Methods) or from those of multiple other participants (Generic ANN).
claims.evidence: This describes two different training approaches for the ANN.

claims.claim: In Exp1, 10 right-handed subjects were tested on 200 possible target locations with the intuitive prosthesis control trained on their own movements.
claims.source: After an initial acquisition in which they picked-and-placed 300 plausible targets with their right arm in a wide workspace, 10 right-handed subjects were tested on 200 possible target locations with our intuitive prosthesis control trained on their own movements (Exp1, TestOwn, Figure 3a) before being tested again on the same targets with their natural arm movements (TestNat).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for Exp1.

claims.claim: In Exp1, median success rate was 100% for TestNat and 99.7% for TestOwn.
claims.source: Results indicate high success rates for both conditions (median success rate of 100% and 99.7% for TestNat and TestOwn, respectively), with a minor (<1%) albeit significant difference between them (TestOwn vs TestNat; n=1886; McNemar test, p=0.023, df = 1; Figure 3b).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from Exp1.

claims.claim: In Exp1, there was a significant difference in success rate between TestOwn and TestNat (p=0.023).
claims.source: Results indicate high success rates for both conditions (median success rate of 100% and 99.7% for TestNat and TestOwn, respectively), with a minor (<1%) albeit significant difference between them (TestOwn vs TestNat; n=1886; McNemar test, p=0.023, df = 1; Figure 3b).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from Exp1.

claims.claim: In Exp1, median movement times were 1.25 s for TestOwn and 1.17 s for TestNat.
claims.source: Regarding movement times (i.e. time taken to reach and validate each target from the previous one), results were also closely similar and not significantly different between conditions (TestOwn vs TestNat; n=10; medians of 1.25 s vs 1.17 s, respectively; two-tailed paired t-test, p=0.378, t=–0.927, df = 9).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from Exp1.

claims.claim: In Exp1, movement times were not significantly different between TestOwn and TestNat (p=0.378).

claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from Exp1.

claims.claim: In Exp1, median shoulder volume was 0.22 dm³ for TestOwn and 0.18 dm³ for TestNat.
claims.source: The volume spread by the shoulder's trajectory throughout a phase, which includes compensatory movements of the body that might be elicited to compensate for imperfect control (see Mick et al., 2021), was also comparable and not significantly different between conditions (TestOwn vs TestNat; n=10; medians of 0.22 dm3 vs 0.18 dm3, respectively; two-tailed paired t-test, p=0.058, t=–2.168, df = 9).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from Exp1.

claims.claim: In Exp1, shoulder volume was not significantly different between TestOwn and TestNat (p=0.058).

claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from Exp1.

claims.claim: The movement-based control trained on the own natural movements of each participant enabled an almost perfect success rate (99.7%).
claims.source: Overall, our movement-based control trained on the own natural movements of each participant enabled an almost perfect success rate (99.7%), and movement times similar to that with their natural arm to pick and place the bottle in the wide workspace tested.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from Exp1.

claims.claim: A critical step toward building an efficient generic model for a new user was to remap hand position data from previous participants to the arm dimensions of that new user.
claims.source: As the relationship between hand locations and arm configurations depends on segment dimensions that differ between participants, a critical step toward building an efficient generic model for a new user was to remap hand position data from previous participants to the arm dimensions of that new user (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
claims.evidence: This describes a methodological approach for the Generic ANN.

claims.claim: Forward kinematics was used to remap data from all participants of Exp1 before using them to train the generic ANN.
claims.source: This was done using forward kinematics to remap data from all participants of Exp1 before using them to train the generic ANN to be used for intuitive control in TestGeneric by each participant of Exp2 (see Methods).
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology for training the Generic ANN.

claims.claim: In Exp2, 12 participants (six left-handed) were tested on the movement-based control using either the generic model or the model based on their own movements.
claims.source: After an initial acquisition phase equivalent to that of Exp1, 12 participants (six left-handed) were tested on our movement-based control using either the generic model (TestGeneric) or the model based on their own movements (TestOwn).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for Exp2.

claims.claim: In Exp2, participants achieved median success rates of 99% or higher in all conditions.
claims.source: Participants achieved high success rates in all conditions (median success rates of 99% or higher, Figure 3b), although minor differences between conditions (<1%) were found significant (TestOwn vs TestGeneric vs TestNat; n=2268; medians of 99.50% vs 99.24% vs 100%, respectively, Cochran's Q test, p=5.19.10–12, Q=51.97, df = 2; post-hoc McNemar test with Bonferroni adjustment; TestOwn vs TestGeneric, p=6.42.10–5, chi.sq=18.1, df = 1; TestOwn vs TestNat, p=8.58.10–3, chi.sq=8.89, df = 1; TestGeneric vs TestNat, p=3.24.10–10, chi.sq=41.7, df = 1).

claims.claim: In Exp2, median success rates were 99.50% for TestOwn, 99.24% for TestGeneric, and 100% for TestNat.

claims.claim: In Exp2, median movement times remained below 1.4 s in all conditions.

claims.claim: In Exp2, there was no significant difference in movement times between conditions (p=0.181).

claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from Exp2.

claims.claim: In Exp2, median shoulder volumes were 0.23 dm³ for TestOwn, 0.43 dm³ for TestGeneric, and 0.14 dm³ for TestNat.
claims.source: With respect to the volume spread by the shoulder during the Test phases (Figure 3d), the statistical analysis revealed a significant effect of condition, (TestOwn vs TestGeneric vs TestNat; medians of 0.23dm3 vs 0.43 dm3 vs 0.14 dm3, respectively, n=12; RM ANOVA test, p=0.003, DFn = 2, DFd = 22, F=7.806), with post-hoc tests indicating a higher volume for TestGeneric than for Test Nat (Tukey test with Bonferroni correction; TestOwn vs TestNat, p=0.385; TestGeneric vs TestNat, p=0.025; TestOwn vs TestGeneric, p=0.347).

claims.claim: In Exp2, there was a significant effect of condition on shoulder volume (p=0.003).

claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from Exp2.

claims.claim: In Exp2, shoulder volume for TestGeneric was significantly higher than for TestNat (p=0.025).

claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from Exp2.

claims.claim: In Exp2, the spread volumes never exceeded 1 liter.
claims.source: Despite this difference, the spread volumes remained contained, never exceeding 1 liter (Figure 3d), which appears reasonable given the high compensations that could have occurred with less efficient controls over the wide workspace spanned by the targets.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative observation from Exp2.

claims.claim: The control based on a generic model enabled new participants to reach almost all targets (>99%) as well as with their natural arm regardless of handedness.
claims.source: Overall, our control based on a generic model trained on data from other participants enabled, therefore, new participants to reach almost all targets (>99%) as well as with their natural arm (or an intuitive control trained on their own natural movements) regardless of handedness, with a moderate increase in compensatory movements.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from Exp2.

claims.claim: Exp3 tested the control on seven participants with unilateral transhumeral limb loss, three of them disabled on their left side.
claims.source: As we now have an intuitive control applicable to participants with an arm amputation on either side of their body, we tested it on seven participants with unilateral transhumeral limb loss, three of them disabled on their left side.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for Exp3.

claims.claim: In Exp3, no initial acquisition phase was conducted on participants with limb loss.
claims.source: As no initial acquisition phase was conducted on these participants, the set of 200 possible targets was determined for each of them using a self-organizing map to extract representative postures from a large number of postures generated by movements produced by all participants of Exp1 filtered to the range of motion of their residual limb (see Methods).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for Exp3.

claims.claim: In Exp3, two blocks of intuitive control with the Generic ANN were conducted on participants' amputated side before they were tested on the same mirrored targets with their valid arm.
claims.source: Therefore, two blocks of intuitive control with the Generic ANN were conducted on their amputated side (TestGeneric 1 and 2, Figure 3), before they were tested on the same mirrored targets with their valid arm (TestNat).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for Exp3.

claims.claim: In Exp3, all median success rates were above 99%.
claims.source: As for other experiments, success rates were very high (all medians above 99%), and did not differ between conditions (TestGeneric1 vs TestGeneric2 vs TestNat; medians of 99.24% vs 99.50% vs 99.50%, respectively, n=1128; Cochran's Q test, p=0.1146, Q=4.33, df = 2).

claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from Exp3.

claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from Exp3.

claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from Exp3.

claims.claim: In Exp3, median shoulder volumes were 0.36 dm³ for TestGeneric1, 0.37 dm³ for TestGeneric2, and 0.33 dm³ for TestNat.
claims.source: The volumes spread by the shoulder were comparable to that measured with the generic model on Exp2 (median 0.43 dm3) and did not differ between conditions (TestGeneric1 vs TestGeneric2 vs TestNat; medians of 0.36 dm3 vs 0.37 dm3 vs 0.33 dm3; n=7; Friedman test, p=0.867, chi-squared=0.28571, df = 2).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from Exp3.

claims.claim: In Exp3, shoulder volumes did not differ between conditions (p=0.867).
claims.source: The volumes spread by the shoulder were comparable to that measured with the generic model on Exp2 (median 0.43 dm3) and did not differ between conditions (TestGeneric1 vs TestGeneric2 vs TestNat; medians of 0.36 dm3 vs 0.37 dm3 vs 0.33 dm3; n=7; Friedman test, p=0.867, chi-squared=0.28571, df = 2).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from Exp3.

claims.claim: Without any prior experience with the task nor with the apparatus, the intuitive control allowed disabled participants to achieve performance as good as with their valid arm.
claims.source: Overall, without any prior experience with the task nor with the apparatus, our intuitive control allowed disabled participants to achieve performance as good as with their valid arm, and to achieve comparable levels of performance as for other subjects in all conditions tested (see Figure 3b–d).
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from Exp3.

claims.claim: A Proof of Concept was conducted whereby 15 participants, including two with acquired and one with congenital transhumeral limb difference, were involved in reaching and grasping real objects.
claims.source: To demonstrate the feasibility of our approach in the physical world, we conducted a Proof of Concept (POC) whereby 15 participants, including two with acquired and one with congenital transhumeral limb difference, were involved in reaching and grasping real objects in various positions and orientations with our novel control applied on a humanoid robotic platform specifically designed to explore human-robot control strategies (Mick et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This describes the physical proof of concept experiment.

claims.claim: In the physical POC, the shoulder flexion-extension and abduction-adduction of the robotic arm were operated from real shoulder movement produced by the operator.
claims.source: As with the Hybrid Arm used to emulate the behavior of an upper arm fitted with a transhumeral prosthesis in virtual reality (Figure 1e), the shoulder flexion-extension and abduction-adduction of the robotic arm were operated from real shoulder movement produced by the operator, whereas the five remaining distal joint angles were driven by prediction from the generic ANN (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This describes the control scheme for the physical POC.

claims.claim: In the physical POC, the torso of the humanoid robotic platform was fixed and independent of the operator.
claims.source: In contrast to virtual reality, however, the torso of the humanoid robotic platform was fixed and independent of the operator, such that compensatory movements from the trunk and from shoulder translations were not transmitted to the device.
claims.evidence: This describes a key difference in the physical POC setup.

claims.claim: In the physical POC, compensatory movements from the trunk and from shoulder translations were not transmitted to the device.
claims.source: In contrast to virtual reality, however, the torso of the humanoid robotic platform was fixed and independent of the operator, such that compensatory movements from the trunk and from shoulder translations were not transmitted to the device.
claims.evidence: This describes a key difference in the physical POC setup.

claims.claim: In the physical POC, high success rates were achieved by all participants in both conditions.
claims.source: Despite the functionality of compensatory movement being withdrawn by design, high success rates were achieved by all participants in both conditions (Figure 4d).
claims.evidence: This is a qualitative result from the physical POC.

claims.claim: In the physical POC, median success rates were 93% for TestGeneric and 100% for TestNat.
claims.source: A significant difference was nevertheless found between the proportion of validated targets using our movement-base control and natural control (TestGeneric vs TestNat; medians 93% vs 100%, respectively; n=180; McNemar test, p=0.0003, chi.sq=13.1, df = 1; Figure 4d).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the physical POC.

claims.claim: In the physical POC, there was a significant difference in success rate between TestGeneric and TestNat (p=0.0003).
claims.source: A significant difference was nevertheless found between the proportion of validated targets using our movement-base control and natural control (TestGeneric vs TestNat; medians 93% vs 100%, respectively; n=180; McNemar test, p=0.0003, chi.sq=13.1, df = 1; Figure 4d).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the physical POC.

claims.claim: In the physical POC, the congenital limb different participant was able to reach and grasp 93.3% of the targets (14/15).
claims.source: The congenital limb different participant was able to reach and grasp 93.3% of the targets (i.e. 14/15), and the two participants with transhumeral limb loss were both able to grasp 80% of the first five targets which means that only one target was failed.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result for a specific participant in the physical POC.

claims.claim: In the physical POC, the two participants with transhumeral limb loss were both able to grasp 80% of the first five targets.
claims.source: The congenital limb different participant was able to reach and grasp 93.3% of the targets (i.e. 14/15), and the two participants with transhumeral limb loss were both able to grasp 80% of the first five targets which means that only one target was failed.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result for specific participants in the physical POC.

claims.claim: In the physical POC, validated targets were reached and grasped with movement times similar to those obtained using natural control applied to the robotic arm.
claims.source: Furthermore, the validated targets were reached and grasped with movement times similar to those obtained using natural control applied to the robotic arm (POCa-b TestGeneric vs TestNat; medians 6.08 s vs 5.98 s, respectively; two-tailed paired t-test, p=0.7026, t=–0.39198, df = 11; Figure 4e).
claims.evidence: This is a comparative result from the physical POC.

claims.claim: In the physical POC, median movement times were 6.08 s for TestGeneric and 5.98 s for TestNat.
claims.source: Furthermore, the validated targets were reached and grasped with movement times similar to those obtained using natural control applied to the robotic arm (POCa-b TestGeneric vs TestNat; medians 6.08 s vs 5.98 s, respectively; two-tailed paired t-test, p=0.7026, t=–0.39198, df = 11; Figure 4e).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the physical POC.

claims.claim: In the physical POC, there was no significant difference in movement times between TestGeneric and TestNat (p=0.7026).
claims.source: Furthermore, the validated targets were reached and grasped with movement times similar to those obtained using natural control applied to the robotic arm (POCa-b TestGeneric vs TestNat; medians 6.08 s vs 5.98 s, respectively; two-tailed paired t-test, p=0.7026, t=–0.39198, df = 11; Figure 4e).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the physical POC.

claims.claim: The first feature that enabled the movement-based control to work well was to introduce the movement goal as an input to the trained ANN.
claims.source: The first feature that enabled our movement-based control to work so well compared to previous attempts was to introduce the movement goal as an input to the trained ANN.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a critical feature of the approach.

claims.claim: Without movement goal as input, the ANN would predict the most likely configuration of the distal joints for a given proximal posture, but irrespective of the location of the object to reach.
claims.source: Without it, the ANN would predict the most likely configuration of the distal joints for a given proximal (shoulder) posture, but irrespective of the location of the object to reach.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a limitation of previous approaches.

claims.claim: The workspace was greatly expanded by starting from the widest possible workspace, limited by the maximal range of motion of participants.
claims.source: First, we greatly expanded the applicable workspace of this control. This was achieved by starting from the widest possible workspace, limited by the maximal range of motion of participants, and subsequently using a self-organizing network (Fritzke, 1994) to best represent the space covered by participants while producing natural arm movements within this space.
claims.evidence: This describes a methodological improvement.

claims.claim: The amount of relevant training data was substantially increased by using the entire trajectories of the recorded natural arm movements.
claims.source: Second, we substantially increased the amount of relevant training data, by using the entire trajectories of the recorded natural arm movements, instead of using only arm postures placing the hand sufficiently close to the target (Mick et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This describes a methodological improvement.

claims.claim: The use of entire trajectories was made efficient by artificially placing the target in the hand.
claims.source: Critically, the use of the entire trajectories was made efficient by artificially placing the target in the hand (see Methods), such that the ANN trained on those data performs a form of natural inverse kinematic solving, i.e., one that provides a solution that is representative of natural arm postures rather than a mere optimization for an arbitrary cost function.
claims.evidence: This describes a methodological innovation.

claims.claim: The control was made applicable to people with limb loss by transferring humeral rotation as an output of the ANN.
claims.source: Here, the humeral rotation was transferred as an output of the ANN, being a predicted output rather than a necessary input for the control system.
claims.evidence: This describes a methodological change to enable applicability to people with limb loss.

claims.claim: A generic control was designed based on natural movements from multiple other individuals, but specifically tuned to the morphology of the user.
claims.source: In addition, instead of training the control on natural arm movements specifically produced by the intended user (also not applicable in people with limb loss), we designed a generic control based on natural movements from multiple other individuals, but specifically tuned to the morphology of the user (see Methods).
claims.evidence: This describes a methodological approach for the Generic ANN.

claims.claim: Specific tuning to the morphology of the user was essential, since a given target position and orientation could call for markedly different arm postures depending on the particular arm morphology of an intended user.
claims.source: This specific tuning was essential, since a given target position and orientation could call for markedly different arm postures depending on the particular arm morphology of an intended user.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a rationale for the morphology-specific tuning.

claims.claim: Mirror symmetry with respect to the medial plane was applied to accommodate for either side of an amputation.
claims.source: Finally, mirror symmetry with respect to the medial plane was applied to accommodate for either side of an amputation.
claims.evidence: This describes a methodological approach to handle different amputation sides.

claims.claim: Including movement goal as an input of the control system could be seen as a weakness, as it might be difficult to determine in real-life settings.
claims.source: Despite the clear benefits mentioned above, including movement goal as an input of the control system could be seen as a weakness, as it might be difficult to determine in real-life settings.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a potential limitation.

claims.claim: Impressive progress in artificial intelligence and computer vision makes determining movement goals appear well within grasp.
claims.source: Yet, impressive progress in artificial intelligence and computer vision is such that what would have been difficult to imagine a decade ago appears now well within grasp (LeCun et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is cited as a reason why the limitation may be overcome.

claims.claim: Deep learning combined with gaze information enables identifying an object that is about to be grasped from an egocentric view on glasses.
claims.source: For instance, we showed recently that deep learning combined with gaze information enables identifying an object that is about to be grasped from an egocentric view on glasses (Pérez de San Roman et al., 2017), and this even in complex cluttered natural environments (González-Díaz et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is cited as evidence that movement goals can be determined.

claims.claim: Six-dimensional object pose estimation is a very active area of computer vision.
claims.source: Six-dimensional object pose estimation is also a very active area of computer vision (Liu, 2022; Nguyen et al., 2022), and prosthesis control strategies based on computer vision combined with gaze and/or myoelectric control for movement intention detection are quickly developing (Starke et al., 2022; Markovic et al., 2015; Krausz et al., 2020; Ghazaei et al., 2017; Mouchoux et al., 2021; He et al., 2020), illustrating the promises of this approach.
claims.evidence: This is cited as evidence of progress in relevant technologies.

claims.claim: Generalizing the approach to multiple tasks including more constrained reaches will require future work.
claims.source: It remains that generalizing our approach to multiple tasks including more constrained reaches will require future work.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a limitation requiring future work.

claims.claim: Further developments are needed to produce natural trajectories compatible with real-world applications.
claims.source: Although our approach enabled participants to converge to the correct position and orientation to grasp simple objects with movement times similar to those of natural movements, it is important to note that further developments are needed to produce natural trajectories compatible with real-world applications.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a limitation requiring future work.

claims.claim: The distal joints predicted by the ANN are realized instantaneously such that a discontinuity occurs at each target change.
claims.source: As easily visible in Videos 2–4, the distal joints predicted by the ANN are realized instantaneously such that a discontinuity occurs at each target change, whereby the distal part of the arm jumps to the novel prediction associated with the new target location.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a current limitation of the approach.

claims.claim: A requirement for the control to be functional on a prosthesis is to have actuated wrist joints available.
claims.source: Another requirement for our control to be functional on a prosthesis is to have actuated wrist joints available, as those are essential to orient the hand in space (Montagnani et al., 2015a; Kanitz et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a requirement for practical implementation.

claims.claim: Most commercial prostheses do not have actuated wrist joints.
claims.source: This is not the case for most commercial prostheses, which sometimes include wrist flexion-extension (mostly passive), and very rarely wrist radial-ulnar deviation (Bajaj et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is cited as a limitation of current commercial prostheses.

claims.claim: The LUKE/DEKA arm includes two wrist degrees of freedom as actuated joints.
claims.source: Notable exceptions include the LUKE/DEKA arm (Resnik et al., 2014a) and the RIC arm (Lenzi et al., 2016), which both include those two degrees of freedom as actuated joints, but with a fixed linear relationship between them.
claims.evidence: This is cited as an exception to the limitation of commercial prostheses.

claims.claim: The solution proposed is suitable to control distal arm joints to place the hand at a correct position and orientation to grasp objects in a wide workspace, but not for fine hand and grasp control involved in object manipulations.
claims.source: As already mentioned, the solution proposed here is suitable to control distal arm joints to place the hand at a correct position and orientation to grasp objects in a wide workspace, but not for fine hand and grasp control involved in object manipulations, which relies heavily on tactile and somatosensory feedback information (Marasco et al., 2021; Marasco et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a scope limitation of the proposed solution.

claims.claim: The movement-based approach appears complementary to more invasive ones, which specifically target hand and grasp functions through bi-directional interactions with the nervous system.
claims.source: In this context, our movement-based approach appears complementary to more invasive ones, which specifically target those latter functions through bi-directional interactions with the nervous system for both motor control and sensory processing (Ortiz-Catalan et al., 2020; Ortiz-Catalan et al., 2014a; D'Anna et al., 2019; Zollo et al., 2019; Salminger et al., 2019).

claims.claim: Combining the movement-based approach with osseointegration at humeral level would restore amplitude and control over shoulder movements.
claims.source: Combining those with osseointegration at humeral level (Ortiz-Catalan et al., 2020; Ortiz-Catalan et al., 2014a) would be particularly relevant as this would also restore amplitude and control over shoulder movements, which are essential for our control but greatly affected by conventional residual limb fitting harnesses and sockets.

claims.claim: The control could be used as is in virtual reality for the management of Phantom-Limb Pain.
claims.source: Besides developments needed for application to a real-life setting, the control proposed here could be used as is in virtual reality for the management of Phantom-Limb Pain (PLP), a painful sensation perceived in the missing limb that often occurs after an amputation.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a potential application.

claims.claim: Reduction of pain has been repeatedly reported using mirror therapy.
claims.source: Although the precise mechanisms behind PLP and its proposed treatments are still debated and unresolved (Di Pino et al., 2021; Makin and Flor, 2020), reduction of pain has been repeatedly reported using mirror therapy, whereby the intact hand is moved while the patient views it through a mirror at the place of his/her missing limb (Chan et al., 2007).

results.result: The authors developed a movement-based prosthesis control system that uses an ANN to predict five distal arm joint angles from shoulder kinematics and target location information. Critical methodological improvements over prior work include: expanding the workspace using self-organizing networks, using entire movement trajectories for training, making humeral rotation an ANN output rather than input, creating a generic model tuned to user morphology, and applying mirror symmetry for either amputation side.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C26, C87-C95 describe the control system design and key methodological innovations. The approach is well-documented with clear rationale (C87-C88, C94) and implementation details (C27-C29, C31, C33-C36, C45-C46). The improvements address specific limitations from prior work (C25) and are supported by the experimental validation that follows.

results.result: Experiment 1 demonstrated that the Own ANN control (trained on each participant's own movements) enabled 10 right-handed participants to achieve near-perfect success rates (99.7%) and movement times (1.25s) statistically indistinguishable from natural arm movements (1.17s, p=0.378) when reaching 200 targets in VR.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C44 provide convergent evidence from Exp1 with appropriate statistical tests (McNemar, paired t-tests) and clear quantitative results. Success rates were very high (>99%), movement times were comparable to natural movements with no significant difference, and shoulder volumes showed minimal compensatory movements. The claim of 'no prior training' (C7) is supported by the experimental design.

results.result: Experiment 2 validated that a Generic ANN (trained on data from other participants but tuned to user morphology) enabled 12 new participants (6 left-handed) to achieve success rates >99% and movement times <1.4s comparable to natural movements, regardless of handedness, though with moderately increased shoulder compensatory movements (0.43 dm³ vs 0.14 dm³, p=0.025).
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C56 demonstrate successful generalization with appropriate statistical analyses (Cochran's Q, RM ANOVA, post-hoc tests). The Generic ANN performed nearly as well as the Own ANN, with only minor differences in success rates (<1%) and a moderate increase in shoulder volume that remained contained (<1 liter). The inclusion of left-handed participants strengthens the generalizability claim.

results.result: Experiment 3 demonstrated that seven participants with transhumeral limb loss achieved performance with the Generic ANN control (success rates >99%, movement times 1.16-1.27s) comparable to or better than their valid arm (1.40s), without any prior training or initial acquisition phase. Participants reported high enthusiasm and found the control intuitive.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C74, C116 provide strong evidence for the primary clinical application. Statistical tests (Cochran's Q, Friedman) show no significant differences in success rates and even faster movement times with practice (TestGeneric2 vs TestNat, p=0.014). The qualitative feedback (C67-C74) corroborates the quantitative findings. However, the small sample size (n=7) and lack of initial acquisition phase (C58) should be noted as limitations for generalizability.

results.result: A physical proof-of-concept demonstrated that 15 participants (including 3 with limb differences) could reach and grasp real objects with a robotic arm using the Generic ANN control, achieving 93% success rate and movement times (6.08s) comparable to natural control (5.98s, p=0.7026), despite the robotic platform preventing compensatory trunk movements.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C86 provide evidence for real-world feasibility. The success rate was lower than in VR (93% vs >99%, p=0.0003) but still high, and movement times were not significantly different. The constraint that trunk movements were not transmitted (C77-C78) strengthens the finding that the control itself is effective. However, the limited testing (only 5 targets for amputees, C83) and lack of statistical analysis for participants with limb differences weakens the generalizability.

results.result: The authors establish the context that controlling multiple prosthetic arm joints remains challenging, with myoelectric control performance deteriorating as DoFs increase (96% to 37% success from 1 to 3 DoFs), and no existing solution for simultaneous intuitive control of four arm DoFs needed for transhumeral prostheses.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C14-C23 accurately cite prior work to establish the problem context. The specific quantitative example (C16) from Nowak et al. 2022 illustrates the performance degradation issue. The anatomical constraints (C17-C18) and limitations of existing approaches (C19-C23) are appropriately referenced. This provides solid motivation for the proposed solution.

results.result: Prior work by the authors (Mick et al., 2021) showed that adding target information to an ANN improved predictions of distal joints from proximal motion, but performance remained lower than natural movements with increased compensatory movements, limited workspace, and inapplicability to people with limb loss.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C25 accurately characterize the authors' prior work and its limitations, providing direct motivation for the current improvements. This is appropriately cited and sets up the methodological advances described in the current study.

results.result: The methods describe the experimental apparatus (VR setup, motion trackers), virtual arm model (7-DoF with three rigid segments), ANN architecture (two 256-neuron layers, dropout, 64-neuron output layer), training parameters (30 epochs at 1e-4 for Own ANN, 10 epochs at 1.59e-7 with 0.95 momentum for Generic ANN), task constraints (2cm/5° hard, 4cm/10° relaxed), and data filtering (removing 3.8% of trials with motion capture errors).
results.evaluation: Claims C30, C32, C125-C134 provide detailed methodological information. The ANN architecture and training parameters are clearly specified (C126-C130), task constraints are defined (C131-C132), and data quality control is documented (C133-C134). The rationale for methodological choices (e.g., C30 explaining joint interdependence) is provided. These details support reproducibility.

results.result: The study included appropriate participant populations across experiments: Exp1 (n=10 right-handed intact-limb), Exp2 (n=12 mixed handedness intact-limb), Exp3 (n=7 transhumeral amputees), and POC (n=15 including 3 with limb differences). All participants provided informed consent and the study was approved by local ethics committee.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C124 document participant demographics and ethical compliance. Sample sizes are modest but reasonable for proof-of-concept work. The inclusion of participants with limb differences in Exp3 and POC is critical for validating the clinical application. Ethical approval and informed consent are properly documented.

results.result: The authors acknowledge that requiring movement goal as input could be seen as a limitation, but argue that advances in computer vision and AI make this feasible. They also note that further work is needed to generalize to multiple tasks, produce natural trajectories, and address the discontinuity in distal joint predictions at target changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C102 appropriately acknowledge limitations and provide balanced discussion. The limitation regarding movement goal input (C96) is countered with evidence of technological feasibility (C97-C99). The acknowledgment of trajectory discontinuities (C102) and need for future work (C100-C101) demonstrates scientific rigor. These are honest assessments of current limitations.

results.result: The authors discuss practical implementation requirements, noting that actuated wrist joints are needed but rare in commercial prostheses (with LUKE/DEKA and RIC arms as exceptions), and that the approach is complementary to invasive neural interfaces focused on hand/grasp control, potentially benefiting from combination with osseointegration or semi-autonomous grasp control.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C110 provide realistic assessment of implementation challenges and integration opportunities. The requirement for actuated wrist joints (C103-C106) is appropriately cited, and the scope limitation regarding hand control (C107) is clearly stated. The discussion of complementary approaches (C108-C110) is speculative but well-reasoned and appropriately cited.

results.result: The authors propose potential applications beyond prosthesis control, including phantom limb pain management in VR (where the control could overcome limitations of mirror therapy for patients with distorted phantom limbs or bilateral limb loss) and augmenting invasive neural interfaces.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C10, C111-C115 propose future applications that are speculative but plausible. The phantom limb pain application (C111-C115) is supported by citations about mirror therapy's limitations and VR's potential, but no data is provided to validate this application. The proposal to augment neural interfaces (C10) is reasonable but untested. These remain hypotheses requiring future validation.

results.result: The field of bionic limbs has seen progress including TMR, osseointegration, and chronically implanted sensors for bidirectional neural communication.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C13 accurately cite established techniques in the field as background context. These are appropriately referenced and provide relevant background for understanding the current state of prosthesis technology.

results.result: The authors developed a novel movement-based prosthesis control system that uses an ANN to predict distal joint angles from proximal shoulder movements and target information. The system was designed to be intuitive and usable without prior training, incorporating several methodological improvements over previous work including expanded workspace, use of entire movement trajectories, morphology-specific tuning, and applicability to people with limb loss.
results.evaluation: Reviewers across all reviews acknowledged the novelty and elegance of the approach. The editor stated 'the provided evidence convincingly demonstrates the approach's feasibility,' and Reviewer 1 noted 'the strength of this paper is that it proposes a method of control for people with transhumeral limb loss which does not rely upon additional surgical intervention.' Reviewer 3 highlighted that 'the approach worked well without requiring user calibration' as 'the most interesting aspect of the work.'

results.result: In Experiment 1, 10 intact-limb participants achieved median success rates of 99.7% with the Own ANN control and 100% with natural movements, with movement times of 1.25s vs 1.17s (not significantly different, p=0.378) and comparable shoulder volumes (0.22 vs 0.18 dm³, p=0.058).
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these specific quantitative results from Exp1. However, Reviewer 1 raised concerns about whether 'movement times in the virtual space would present a very different distribution to natural movements, while the mean values could be similar,' requesting 'individual participant data showing distributions of movement times.' This suggests acceptance of the reported values but questions about their interpretation.

results.result: In Experiment 2, 12 participants (including left-handed) tested both Generic and Own ANN models, achieving success rates >99% in all conditions with movement times below 1.4s (no significant difference, p=0.181). The Generic model showed moderately increased shoulder volume (0.43 dm³) compared to natural movements (0.14 dm³, p=0.025), but volumes never exceeded 1 liter.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these results without direct challenge. Reviewer 2 expressed intrigue about 'how the Generic ANN model has been trained' and suggested alternative approaches like 'few shot calibration methods,' but did not dispute the reported performance. The moderate increase in compensatory movements was acknowledged by the authors and appears accepted by reviewers as reasonable given the wide workspace.

results.result: In Experiment 3, seven participants with transhumeral limb loss achieved success rates >99% without prior training using the Generic ANN, with movement times in the second block (1.16s) significantly faster than their valid arm (1.40s, p=0.014). Participants provided enthusiastic qualitative feedback about the intuitiveness of the control.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged this as a strength. Reviewer 3 noted 'the work was also tested with a reasonable number of subjects, including those with limb-loss' and that 'the approach worked well without requiring user calibration.' The qualitative feedback was not challenged, though Reviewer 2 questioned whether 'no familiarisation would be needed' if the method is truly 'intuitive,' suggesting some uncertainty about the interpretation of 'no training.'

results.result: A physical proof-of-concept demonstrated that 15 participants (including 3 with limb differences) could reach and grasp real objects with a robotic arm using the movement-based control. Success rates were 93% with the Generic control vs 100% with natural control (p=0.0003), with similar movement times (6.08s vs 5.98s, p=0.7026).
results.evaluation: While reviewers acknowledged the physical demonstration, they raised significant concerns about its limitations. Reviewer 1 noted 'the teleoperation proof of concept of movement based control does not seem to feature a similar range of object distance from the user as the virtual environment' and emphasized that 'real world prosthesis control introduces numerous challenges which do not exist in virtual spaces or in teleoperation robotics.' Reviewer 3 pointed out the device was tested 'without it being physically attached to the user' and that 'the weight of a device attached to a user will impact the shoulder movements.'

results.result: Movement times with the control system were comparable to natural movements across all experiments, with typical times around 1.3s in virtual reality and 6s in the physical proof-of-concept.
results.evaluation: Reviewers questioned the interpretation of movement time results. Reviewer 1 raised concerns about whether the ANN's instantaneous predictions might artificially reduce movement times: 'at the start of each trial period, either pick or place, the ANN appears to have already selected the position of the five joints it controls, leaving the user to position the upper arm such that the end effector reaches the target.' They suggested 'individual participant data showing distributions of movement times' would better support the claims. The editor noted the approach demonstrates 'feasibility' but requires 'additional improvements' for 'practical requirements.'

results.result: The authors acknowledge limitations including the reliance on target information as input, the need for natural trajectories rather than instantaneous jumps, and the need to generalize to multiple tasks and more constrained reaches. They argue that advances in computer vision and AI make target detection feasible.
results.evaluation: Reviewers emphasized these limitations as significant concerns. Reviewer 1 stated 'it can be argued that a great many problems in upper limb prosthesis control can be solved given precise knowledge of the object to be grasped, its relative position in 3D space and its orientation' and that 'scaling this approach to work robustly in a real world environment will necessitate solving a number of challenges in machine learning and in particular computer vision which are not trivial in nature.' Reviewer 3 noted 'the reliance on target position is a complicating factor in deploying this technology.' The editor concluded 'additional improvements are needed for this proof-of-concept neuro-model to fulfil practical requirements.'

results.result: The workspace was expanded by generating 300 'plausible' targets within full range of motion, then using a self-organizing network to identify 200 'possible' targets that represent arm postures actually produced by participants during natural movements.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge this methodological approach. Reviewer 3 noted 'the authors did a nice job spanning the workspace,' though they added concerns about whether 'the unconstrained nature of reaches could make restoring additional activities problematic.'

results.result: The control requires actuated wrist joints (flexion-extension and radial-ulnar deviation) which are not available in most commercial prostheses, though exceptions like the LUKE/DEKA and RIC arms exist.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged this hardware limitation. Reviewer 2 noted 'the availability of prosthetic hardware that offers such functionality' as one of the 'limitations/challenges that the approach suffers from.' This limitation was accepted as a practical constraint rather than a flaw in the research.

results.result: The authors propose that their control is complementary to other approaches, suitable for arm positioning but not fine hand control, and could be combined with invasive neural interfaces, osseointegration, semi-autonomous grasp control, or used for phantom limb pain management in VR.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these as reasonable future directions and applications. Reviewer 2 suggested the authors 'could also briefly discuss how they foresee the method could be expanded to enable a grasp command beyond the proximity between the end-point and the target,' indicating interest in these complementary approaches. Reviewer 3 noted the approach 'could be used to help complete meaningful functional activities of daily living that require semi-consistent movements, such as feeding and grooming.'

results.result: The study included appropriate participant demographics across experiments (29 total participants including 7 with limb loss) with proper ethical approvals.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge the participant demographics or ethical compliance. The sample sizes were implicitly accepted as adequate, with Reviewer 3 noting 'the work was also tested with a reasonable number of subjects, including those with limb-loss.'

results.result: The methods describe the virtual arm model, ANN architecture (two 256-neuron layers, dropout, 64-neuron layer), training parameters (30 epochs for Own ANN, 10 for Generic ANN with specific learning rates), task constraints (2cm/5° hard, 4cm/10° relaxed), and data filtering (removing 3.8% of trials with motion capture errors).
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these methodological details. Reviewer 2 expressed interest in understanding 'the relative importance of the target information versus body posture in the estimation of the arm position' and how to 'distinguish' this 'beyond looking at the weights in the neural network,' but did not dispute the methods themselves.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluations support the methodological approach and control system design (C2, C26, C33-C36, C87-C95). OpenEval emphasizes the well-documented rationale and implementation details, while peer reviewers highlight the novelty, elegance, and lack of required surgical intervention. Both agree on the strength of the approach, though peer reviewers focus more on the no-calibration aspect (C7, C8) which OpenEval addresses separately in R2.

Both evaluations support the Exp1 results (C3-C5, C37-C44) showing high success rates and comparable movement times. However, peer reviewers raise concerns about the interpretation of movement time distributions, requesting individual participant data to verify that distributions (not just means) are similar to natural movements. OpenEval accepts the statistical results without this caveat.

Both evaluations support the generalization results from Exp2 (C47-C56), showing the Generic ANN performed nearly as well as Own ANN. OpenEval provides detailed statistical validation, while peer reviewers accept the results and express interest in the training methodology. Both acknowledge the moderate increase in compensatory movements as reasonable.

Both evaluations support the clinical application results from Exp3 (C57-C74, C116). OpenEval notes the small sample size as a limitation but finds the evidence strong. Peer reviewers acknowledge this as a strength, particularly the no-calibration aspect, though Reviewer 2 questions the interpretation of 'no training' versus 'no familiarization.' Both agree on the positive qualitative feedback.

OpenEval supports the real-world feasibility results (C6, C75-C86) while noting limited testing as a weakness. Peer reviewers are more uncertain, raising significant concerns about the teleoperation setup not being physically attached to users, the limited range of object distances, and the impact of device weight on shoulder movements. Both note the lower success rate compared to VR, but peer reviewers emphasize practical deployment challenges more strongly.

Both address limitations regarding movement goal input and real-world deployment (C96-C102). OpenEval views the acknowledgment of limitations as demonstrating scientific rigor and finds the discussion balanced. Peer reviewers are more uncertain, emphasizing these as significant concerns for practical deployment, particularly the reliance on precise target position knowledge and the non-trivial computer vision challenges. The editor concludes additional improvements are needed.

Both evaluations support the participant demographics and ethical compliance (C117-C124). OpenEval finds the sample sizes reasonable for proof-of-concept work, and peer reviewers explicitly note the work was tested with a reasonable number of subjects including those with limb loss. No concerns were raised by either evaluation.

Both evaluations support the detailed methodological specifications (C30, C32, C125-C134).
